title: Surviving the winter: hibernation and other resting states

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In winter, many animals become inactive for periods of varying duration. There are various words used to describe this state, including sleep, dormancy, lethargy and hibernation. Hibernation is often used loosely to refer to general inactivity. However, in biology this word refers to the specific condition of passing the winter in a resting state of deep sleep, during which metabolic rate* and body temperature drop considerably.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: In hibernating animals, body temperature falls from around 38°C to about 1°C above the external temperature, which is often close to 0°C. At the same time, the animal's metabolic rate falls to as little as 1% of its normal value. The heartbeat becomes slow and irregular, and breathing rate also slows.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Hibernation is an active process. It is a state that animals enter into in response to internal stimuli, rather than immediate external conditions. Some animals are remarkably precise and predictable. For example, the arctic ground squirrel enters hibernation between 5 and 12 October, regardless of the weather on those dates. This behaviour differs from other sleepy states, which are an immediate response to current conditions. Brown and black bears, for example, are lethargic during very cold periods, but are otherwise active in the winter. Another feature of hibernation that distinguishes it from other kinds of winter inactivity is that hibernators can arouse themselves spontaneously, and are not dependent on external conditions, such as warm temperatures, to do so. The arctic ground squirrel emerges without fail between 20 and 22 April.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: True hibernation occurs only in certain mammals, and one bird species, the poorwill, a North American relative of the nightjar. Only relatively small mammals hibernate, though not all small mammals living in temperate habitats hibernate during winter. The largest mammal to hibernate is the marmot, which weighs about 5 kg. There are several reasons why larger mammals do not hibernate during their lifetime. Firstly, they would warm up too slowly, and therefore use too much energy. Secondly, they have a smaller surface area to volume ratio, and so can conserve body heat better than smaller species. Finally, they are better able to carry a thick coat and fat, to last through the winter. Hibernators are mainly found amongst rodents, bats and insectivore** species. The hedgehog is an example of a hibernating insectivore.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The physiological features that are characteristic of hibernation are not maintained throughout the winter. Rather, the animal wakes up at intervals, and its temperature and metabolic rate increase to near-normal levels. The function of this intermittent arousal is not wholly clear. Some species, such as the chipmunk, eat from stored food reserves during arousal, but many others do not. Most species urinate, defecate and move about and change their position, suggesting that arousal provides an opportunity for various physiological processes to be performed, and to prevent the animal from dying. Calculations done in laboratory studies of the ground squirrel show that during the relatively brief periods of arousal, an individual animal expends 83% of all the energy that it uses up during the entire hibernation period.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Hibernation requires internal energy reserves in the form of fat, and hibernators typically feed intensively prior to winter, building up their fat stores. Some species, such as the edible dormouse, switch to a diet which is rich in carbohydrates and fats, e.g. seeds, at this time of their life.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Hibernation seems to be a safe, rather pleasant way to spend the winter, but for some species it is fraught with danger. For Belding's ground squirrels living at high altitudes in Tioga Pass, California, hibernation lasts 7 – 8 months. Two-thirds of all juveniles, hibernating for the first time, and one-third of adult animals die during hibernation. Some die because their fat reserves run out before the end of hibernation; others are dug up and eaten by predators. Some animals spend the winter in groups, huddled together, and so conserve body heat. North American raccoons, for example, spend hibernation periods in communal dens.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: For some mammals, resting states are closely associated with other important activities, notably reproduction and migration. For example, brown bears living at northern latitudes mate in the autumn and give birth to their cubs during winter lethargy, while edible dormice and some types of bat mate immediately after the end of hibernation. Dispersal is an important part of the life history of many animals, especially mammals; some migrate permanently from their place of birth, usually at the end of the breeding season. However, dispersal is potentially both dangerous and energetically expensive because mammals at this time tend to be vulnerable to predators and, being on the move, have little time to feed. Dispersal therefore requires internal energy reserves, the very same ones that the animals may need later to survive the winter. There may thus be a trade-off between dispersal and hibernation in the allocation of energy reserves.
